meaning: A rhetorical question used as a strong denial: “no way I'd ...”, “as if ...”. It carries determination or a sharp rebuttal.
connection: Verb dictionary form／い-adj.／な-adj. + な + ものか (casual: もんか; polite: ものですか)

senses.label: Never! (determination)
senses.meaning: The speaker uses a rhetorical question to say they will absolutely not do something. The tone is strong, often angry or defiant. Often paired with 「二度と」 or 「絶対」.
senses.connection: Volitional verb dictionary form + ものか／もんか (e.g. 「行くもんか」, 「負けるものか」)
examples: I'll never go to that shop again.
There's no way I'm losing here!

senses.label: As if ... (rebuttal)
senses.meaning: A rhetorical question that denies what someone said or rejects a possibility, like “as if ...” or “how could ...?”. 「ものですか」 is softer and more often used by women.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／い-adj.／な-adj. + な + ものか／ものですか
examples: As if that could ever happen.
A problem this hard? No way a child could understand it.
Him, kind? Hardly.

notes: Angry or defiant, and very strong. Saying 「そんなこと、知るもんか」 to a superior or client is extremely rude. To deny politely, say 「そのようなことはございません」 or 「〜とは思えません」.
「ものか」 already carries the negation, so it attaches to an affirmative form: ✕「二度と行かないものか」 (this becomes 「〜ないものか」, “isn't there some way not to go?”) → ○「二度と行くものか」.
Let the pitch fall at the end of the sentence. With rising intonation it sounds like a genuine question, and the denial and resolve do not come through.
「もんか」 is rough and used mostly by men or in quarrels; 「ものですか」 is only slightly softer and is still a strong denial, so it does not suit formal settings.

daily.title: Swearing off a place
daily.description: You were treated badly at a shop and tell a friend you're never going back.
daily.example: A rude place like that? I'm never going there again.

daily.title: Pumping yourself up
daily.description: You're about to lose a match and grit your teeth.
daily.example: I've come this far. I'm not giving up now.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Characters in novels often use 「ものか」 to show strong emotion when they push back.
daily.example: “What would you know?” he shouted.

work.title: Venting to a coworker
work.description: After unfair criticism, you complain privately to a coworker you trust.
work.example: After being talked to like that, how could I just stay quiet?

etymology: The formal noun 「もの」 plus the question particle 「か」. The rhetorical question “Is there such a thing?” turns into a denial. 「もんか」 is the spoken sound change of 「ものか」.

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: Both can mean “impossible”. 「〜わけがない」 is a calm, logical judgment with no anger. To state your own resolve never to do something, only 「〜ものか」 works (「二度と行くものか」); you cannot replace it with 「〜わけがない」.

similar.title: 〜まい
similar.explanation: 「〜まい」 can also express resolve (「二度と行くまい」), but it is mostly written or an inner monologue, and calm and restrained. 「〜ものか」 is a rhetorical question spoken aloud, full of anger or defiance.

similar.title: 〜っこない
similar.explanation: 「〜っこない」 is also a spoken “no way” (「勝てっこない」). It attaches to the stem of the verb (ます-stem) and only denies possibility; it cannot express resolve. 「〜ものか」 can express both.

similar.title: 〜ないものか・〜ないものだろうか
similar.explanation: Same origin: also built from 「もの」 + 「か」, but after a negative form, expressing the wish “isn't there some way to ...?” (「何とかならないものか」). The single 「ない」 makes the meaning almost the opposite.

formation: 「ものか」 is the formal noun 「もの」 plus the sentence-final particle 「か」. 「もの」 sums up what comes before as “such a thing”, and 「か」 asks a rhetorical question: “Would there be such a thing?” The obvious answer is “no”, so the whole phrase becomes a strong denial. When the speaker is the subject and the verb is volitional, “Would I do such a thing?” turns into resolve: “I'll never do it.” When it is about someone else or about things, it becomes a rebuttal: “How could that be?” Because the denial is made through the rhetorical question, an affirmative form must come before it, and the pitch falls at the end. 「もんか」 is the spoken contraction, and 「ものですか」 adds 「です」 and is a little more polite.

meaning: The speaker strongly senses a certain quality in something: “there is something ... about it”, “it really is ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form／い-adj.／な-adj. + な + ものがある

senses.label: Moving
senses.meaning: Something touches your heart: “there is something moving about ...”. Often used with 「胸に迫る」, 「心を打つ」 or 「訴える」.
senses.connection: 「胸に迫る」, 「心を打つ」, 「訴える」, 「感じる」, etc. + ものがある／ものがあった
examples: There was something deeply moving about his speech.
There's something touching about this movie.
His work has something that speaks to people's hearts.

senses.label: Remarkable degree
senses.meaning: The speaker evaluates something and says it is quite strong or striking. The tone is objective and understated, softer than stating it directly.
senses.connection: 「目を見張る」, 「難しい」, 「大変な」, 「相当な」, etc. + ものがある
examples: The young players' growth is truly remarkable.
Raising a child alone is really tough.
Making this plan happen in a year would be quite difficult.

notes: It must follow a word of feeling or evaluation (「胸に迫る」, 「目を見張る」, 「難しい」). After an ordinary verb it is just literal: 「冷蔵庫に食べるものがある」 means “there is something to eat in the fridge”, not this grammar point.
It mostly evaluates things such as works, performances or changes. To describe a person's character, use 「ところがある」: ✕「彼には優しいものがある」 → ○「彼には優しいところがある」.
It has a critic's tone. Telling a superior or client 「なかなか見事なものがありますね」 about their work sounds condescending; state your feeling directly instead (「本当に感動しました」).

daily.title: Talking about a movie
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about a film you just saw.
daily.example: There was something really moving about that last scene, wasn't there?

daily.title: Reading a review
daily.description: Book and film reviews often use this pattern for a subtle evaluation.
daily.example: That piece of writing has something that grabs the reader.

work.title: Praising a team member
work.description: A manager acknowledges a new employee's progress in a meeting.
work.example: The new hire's progress is truly impressive.

work.title: News and commentary
work.description: A commentator points out a serious situation in an understated way.
work.example: The impact of the weak yen on household budgets is quite serious.

etymology: The formal noun 「もの」 means “something, some element”. With 「がある」, it says “there is something (in it)”. From this comes “there really is something ... about it”.

similar.title: 〜ものだ（感慨・当然・回想）
similar.explanation: Same origin; both use the formal noun 「もの」 to express feeling. 「〜ものだ」 is the speaker's direct exclamation (「早いものだ」); 「〜ものがある」 says “this thing has a certain quality”, which is more indirect and more like a review.

similar.title: 〜だけのことはある
similar.explanation: Also high praise, but 「〜だけのことはある」 stresses “as befits their status or effort; they live up to their reputation”, so there is a cause-and-effect link (「プロだけのことはある」). 「〜ものがある」 only expresses the quality you sense, without giving a reason.

similar.title: 〜といったらない
similar.explanation: 「〜といったらない」 also means an extreme degree, but it is exaggerated and openly emotional, mostly about the speaker's own feelings (「悔しいといったらない」). 「〜ものがある」 is restrained and indirect, mostly used in writing to evaluate its object.

formation: 「ものがある」 is the formal noun 「もの」 plus 「がある」. Here 「もの」 is not a concrete object but “some quality or element that is hard to pin down”, so 「〜には…ものがある」 literally says “within ... there exists something ...”. Instead of saying outright “it's moving” or “it's difficult”, the speaker says “there is something moving / difficult in it”, turning a subjective judgment into a description of the thing's nature. This makes the tone indirect and objective, suited to reviews and speeches. And because it points out an element contained in the subject, the preceding word must express a feeling or evaluation, such as 「胸に迫る」 or 「目を見張る」.

title: 〜ものだ (feelings / common sense / memories)
meaning: Expresses the nature of things or common sense, the speaker's deep feelings, nostalgic memories of what used to happen, and advice about what one should do.
connection: Verb dictionary form／ta-form／nai-form, い-adj., な-adj. + な + ものだ (casual: もんだ)

senses.label: Nature / common sense
senses.meaning: The basic nature of things or a general social truth: “that's just how ... is”. It is about a general rule, not one specific event.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／nai-form + ものだ (often with 「人は」 or 「〜とは」)
examples: People's feelings change. That's just how it is.
Kids just don't listen to their parents.

senses.label: Deep feeling
senses.meaning: The speaker expresses heartfelt amazement: “how ... it is!”. Often used with 「本当に」, 「よく」 and a final 「ね」 or 「なあ」.
senses.connection: い-adj.／な-adj. + な + ものだ (ね／なあ)
examples: Time really flies.
Life is a strange thing, isn't it?

senses.label: Fond memories
senses.meaning: Looking back with nostalgia on something you used to do often: “I used to ...”. Often with 「よく」, 「昔は」 or 「子供のころ」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ものだ
examples: When I was a kid, I used to swim in this river all the time.
In my student days, we would talk late into the night.

senses.label: What one should do
senses.meaning: Based on common sense or manners, says what one “should” do. Used for advice or lessons. Softer than 「べきだ」, with a sense of “that's just common sense”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ものだ (negative: 「〜ものではない」)
examples: When someone gives you something, you should thank them.
You should use keigo with your seniors.

notes: The form decides the meaning: 「よく行ったものだ」 means “I used to go often” (recollection), while 「行くものだ」 means “one should go / people naturally go” (advice, general truth). Changing the た-form to the dictionary form changes the meaning completely.
The “as it should be” use sounds preachy. Saying 「〜するものですよ」 to a superior or client is very rude, and to a junior it can also sound condescending.
The recollection use is only for things repeated or habitual in the past, not one-time events: ✕「去年一度京都へ行ったものだ」 → ○「去年京都へ行った」.
「〜たいものだ」 is a strong wish (「一度行ってみたいものだ」), not a recollection. 「たい」 and 「た」 differ by one letter, so distinguish them when listening and reading.

daily.title: At a class reunion
daily.description: Meeting old classmates after many years and looking back.
daily.example: We used to play here together all the time, didn't we?

daily.title: At the end of the year
daily.description: Telling your family how fast the year went.
daily.example: A year goes by in the blink of an eye, doesn't it?

daily.title: Teaching manners
daily.description: A parent teaches a child basic manners.
daily.example: You're supposed to say 「いただきます」 before you eat.

work.title: A senior coworker's advice
work.description: A senior coworker explains workplace common sense to a newcomer.
work.example: You should get to meetings with clients a little early.

work.title: A speech
work.description: A farewell speech at a retirement party, reflecting on the years.
work.example: Thirty years seems long, but looking back, it went by quickly.

etymology: 「もの」 was originally written 「物」, meaning “thing”. As a formal noun it refers to the general nature of things. With 「だ」, it means “that's just how it is”. The uses for feelings, memories and advice grew out of this.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: Both can mean “should”. 「〜べきだ」 is the speaker's own firm claim; 「〜ものだ」 relies on “that is just what common sense says”, so it is softer, but equally preachy.

similar.title: 〜たものだ（回想）
similar.explanation: Same origin: it refers specifically to the recollection use of 「た-form + ものだ」, with a note of nostalgia. To merely state a past habit you can use 「〜ていた」, which has no emotional coloring.

similar.title: 〜というものだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜というものだ」 means “that is what ... is” or “that is what we call ...”, a judgment about the essence of something (「それが友情というものだ」). 「〜ものだ」 states general truths or expresses emotion.

similar.title: 〜ものではない
similar.explanation: Same origin: this is the negative of this grammar point. The negative of the advice use 「〜ものだ」 (“should”) is 「〜ものではない」 (“should not”), not 「〜ないものだ」.

formation: 「ものだ」 is the formal noun 「もの」 plus the copula 「だ」. The noun 「もの」 originally means “thing”, but as a formal noun it refers to “the general nature or usual state of things”. So 「〜ものだ」 means “that is just the kind of thing it is”, presenting a matter as a general rule. State the rule directly and you get the general-truth use; tell it to the listener as “that is how it ought to be” and you get advice; exclaim “so that's how it is!” about what is in front of you and you get emotion; attach it to the た-form and fondly recall past repeated events as “how things used to be” and you get recollection. All four uses come from the same core idea of summing a matter up as a general state.

meaning: Warns someone, based on common sense, that they shouldn't do something. It can also mean something is by nature impossible or hard.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ものではない (casual: もんじゃない)

senses.label: Shouldn't
senses.meaning: Warns or criticizes someone, based on social norms or morals: “you shouldn't ...”. Usually said by an older person to a younger one.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ものではない／ものではありません／もんじゃない
examples: You shouldn't speak ill of others.
You shouldn't go out alone late at night.
You must not talk like that to your elders.

senses.label: Just can't be done
senses.meaning: By the nature of things, something simply can't happen or isn't that easy. Often with 「そう簡単に」 or 「なかなか」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／potential form + ものではない
examples: A person's character doesn't change that easily.
You can't learn a foreign language in a day.

notes: The admonishing use lectures from the standpoint of common sense, so use it only to juniors, children or very close people. Saying 「〜するものではありません」 to a superior or client is very rude.
One extra 「た」 changes the meaning completely: 「簡単に食べられるものではない」 means “it's not something you can easily eat”, while 「食べられたものではない」 means “it's so bad it's inedible”.
To deny a one-sided view you must add 「という」: ✕「お金があればいいものではない」 → ○「お金があればいいというものではない」 (it's not enough just to have money).
The admonishing use attaches to the dictionary form: ✕「そんなことを言ったものではない」 → ○「そんなことを言うものではない」.

daily.title: Teaching a child
daily.description: A parent sees a child wasting food and scolds them.
daily.example: You must not waste food.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: A friend complains that practice isn't paying off, and you tell them to be patient.
daily.example: Skills don't come overnight, you know.

work.title: A senior coworker's reminder
work.description: A junior looked at their phone in front of a client. The senior mentions it afterwards.
work.example: You shouldn't look at your phone in front of clients.

work.title: In a report or essay
work.description: An essay points out that a problem can't be solved easily.
work.example: The low birthrate problem is not something that can be solved in a short time.

etymology: The negative of 「ものだ」 (common sense, what should be). 「ものだ」 means “that's how it should be”; in the negative it becomes “that's not how it should be” or “that just doesn't happen”.

similar.title: 〜べきではない
similar.explanation: Both mean “should not”. 「〜べきではない」 is the speaker's subjective judgment and works in formal arguments and opinions; 「〜ものではない」 admonishes on the basis of common sense, mostly from elders to juniors, and is more colloquial.

similar.title: 〜てはならない
similar.explanation: 「〜てはならない」 means “absolutely forbidden” by rules or morality, in a solemn, stern tone, mostly in regulations and instructions. 「〜ものではない」 is the milder admonition “one doesn't do that, as a rule”.

similar.title: 〜たものではない
similar.explanation: Same origin: after the た-form of a potential verb (「見られたものではない」), it means “it's terrible, not fit to ...”, a strongly negative evaluation, not an admonition.

similar.title: 〜というものではない
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜というものではない」 means “it's not the case that ... is enough”, denying a one-sided view (「高ければいいというものではない」). 「〜ものではない」 admonishes or explains the nature of things.

formation: 「ものではない」 is the negative of 「ものだ」. 「ものだ」 says “that is how things are by nature (general truth)”, so the negative says “that is not how things are by nature”. About a person's action, “that is not something one (a decent person) does” becomes an admonition: “you shouldn't ...”. About the nature of a thing, “it is not that kind of thing by nature” becomes “it doesn't ... / it isn't easy to ...”. Because it rests on “common sense” rather than the speaker's personal opinion, it sounds like an elder explaining how things are, with a hint of condescension.

meaning: Gives a reason, usually when making excuses or apologizing. It sounds soft and suggests “I couldn't help it”.
connection: Verb・い-adj. plain form／な-adj. + な／noun + な + もので (casual: もんで)

senses.label: Excuses / apologies
senses.meaning: Explains the reason for your mistake or rudeness and asks for understanding. Softer than 「から」 or 「ので」. The second half is often an apology or something that already happened.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form／ていた + もので、〜 (すみません／申し訳ありません)
examples: The roads were crowded, so I'm late.
I was in a hurry, so I forgot to contact you.

senses.label: Explaining your situation
senses.meaning: Humbly explains your situation to say why you can't do something: “since ...”. Often used to decline or ask for understanding.
senses.connection: Verb・い-adj. plain form／noun + な + もので、〜
examples: I'm still not used to things, so I'm sorry for any trouble.
My kids are still small, so I can't go out at night.
I'm just a country person, so I don't know much about city life.

notes: The second clause cannot be a command, request, invitation or statement of will: ✕「寒いもので、窓を閉めてください」 → ○「寒いので、窓を閉めていただけますか」.
It suits explaining your own circumstances to ask for understanding. Giving only a reason without an apology (ending 「道が混んでいたもので」 with no 「申し訳ありません」) is taken in Japan as making an excuse.
Not for objective cause and effect: ✕「雨が降ったもので、地面が濡れている」 → ○「雨が降ったので、地面が濡れている」.
Nouns and な-adjectives take 「な」: ○「初めてなもので」, 「田舎者なもので」.

daily.title: Late to meet a friend
daily.description: Explaining to a friend why you're late.
daily.example: The trains had stopped, so I was late. Sorry!

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: A neighbor invites you to a party and you politely explain.
daily.example: I have an early morning tomorrow, so I'll head home now.

work.title: Apologizing to a client
work.description: Explaining a late reply at the start of an email.
work.example: I was on a business trip, so I apologize for the late reply.

work.title: A newcomer explains
work.description: A new employee explains a mistake to a senior coworker.
work.example: I'm still not used to things, so I didn't check carefully enough.

etymology: The formal noun 「もの」 plus 「で」, the connective form of 「だ」, meaning “it's that kind of situation”. Giving the reason in this noun-like way sounds softer.

similar.title: 〜ものだから
similar.explanation: Same origin, almost the same meaning. 「〜ものだから」 is more colloquial and stresses the reason more; 「〜もので」 is shorter and crisper, and more common in business apologies.

similar.title: 〜ので
similar.explanation: 「〜ので」 states a cause objectively and has wide use; the second clause can be a request. 「〜もので」 carries an excuse-like “I couldn't help it, please understand”, and the second clause cannot be a request or command.

similar.title: 〜もの・〜もん（言い訳）
similar.explanation: Same origin: sentence-final 「〜もの・〜もん」 is a childlike excuse (「知らなかったんだもん」), used only among intimates. 「〜もので」 comes mid-sentence and can be used in polite situations.

formation: 「もので」 is the formal noun 「もの」 plus 「で」, the continuative form of the copula 「だ」; literally “it's like this, so ...”. Instead of a bare “because of A”, the reason is packaged as “a settled situation I can't help”, which lightens the speaker's responsibility and gives a tone of explanation and a plea for understanding. And since it is “explaining the situation”, the second clause can only be a result that has already happened or the speaker's own condition, not a request or command to the other person. It lacks the 「から」 of 「ものだから」, so it is shorter and sounds crisper and more proper.

meaning: Imagines something very hard to achieve: “if only I could ..., I would ...”. Can also be a challenge: “go ahead, try it if you can”.
connection: Verb potential form／dictionary form + ものなら (casual: もんなら)

senses.label: Unlikely wish
senses.meaning: Imagines something nearly impossible and expresses a strong wish: “if I could ...”. The second half usually has 「〜たい」 or 「〜てほしい」.
senses.connection: Verb potential form + ものなら、〜たい (「できる」, 「戻れる」, 「行ける」, etc.)
examples: If I could, I'd love to go back to my student days.
If I could go, I'd fly there right now.
If I could start over, I would.

senses.label: Challenge
senses.meaning: You think the other person can't do it, and you dare them: “go ahead, try it”. A blunt, spoken expression.
senses.connection: Verb potential form + ものなら、〜てみろ／〜てみなさい
examples: Do it if you can.
Go on, say it if you dare.

notes: The two meanings differ completely depending on the form: 「行けるものなら行きたい」 is “if I could go, I'd like to”, while 「遅刻しようものなら怒られる」 is “if I should be late, I'll be scolded”.
Use it only for things the speaker thinks are hard to achieve. For things you can do any time, use 「〜たら」 or 「〜なら」: ✕「明日も会えるものなら会いたい」 (when you can meet tomorrow anyway).
The challenge 「やれるものならやってみろ」 is very aggressive. Used toward a superior, client or stranger it causes a clash; keep it to quarrels or joking among friends.
The second clause is the speaker's wish or challenge (「〜たい」, 「〜てみろ」), not an objective statement: ✕「行けるものなら、彼は行く」.

daily.title: Missing the old days
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about school days.
daily.example: If only I could go back to high school.

daily.title: Siblings teasing
daily.description: An older brother doesn't believe his little brother can do it and goads him.
daily.example: If you can eat it all by yourself, go ahead and try.

daily.title: Missing family far away
daily.description: Working abroad and missing your family.
daily.example: If I could, I'd go home right now to see my family.

work.title: After a failed project
work.description: Opening up to coworkers over drinks after a project failed.
work.example: If I could turn back time, I'd redo that decision.

etymology: The formal noun 「もの」 plus the conditional 「なら」. 「もの」 makes the supposed situation feel out of reach, which gives the sense of “it's actually hard to do”.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うものなら
similar.explanation: Same origin, and the most easily confused. It attaches to the volitional form and means “if one should do ..., serious consequences follow” (「遅刻しようものなら、怒られる」); 「〜ものなら」 attaches to the potential form and expresses a hard-to-fulfil wish or a challenge.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「〜なら」 is an ordinary conditional with no sense of “almost impossible”. 「〜ものなら」 stresses that the premise is hard to realize, and the second clause is mostly a strong wish.

similar.title: 〜たいものだ・〜てほしいものだ
similar.explanation: Same origin; both express a strong wish with 「もの」. 「〜たいものだ」 says outright “I'd really like to ...” (「一度行ってみたいものだ」); 「〜ものなら」 first supposes “if it were really possible” and then states the wish, stressing how hard it is.

formation: 「ものなら」 is the formal noun 「もの」 plus the conditional particle 「なら」. 「なら」 sets up a hypothesis, “if that is the case”, and 「もの」 abstracts its content into “such a thing”, putting distance from reality and hinting that “in fact it is hardly possible”. So a potential form usually comes before it: “if one could really do such a thing ...”, and the second clause naturally expresses the speaker's wish 「〜たい」. Throw the same hypothesis at the other person, “if you can really do it (I don't believe you can)”, and it becomes the challenge 「〜てみろ」.

title: 〜もの・〜もん (excuses)
meaning: Placed at the end of a sentence to give a reason, with a whiny, defensive or “you get it, right?” tone: “but ...!”, “because ..., you know”.
connection: Plain form (noun・な-adj. + だ)／〜んだ + もの・もん

senses.label: Whiny excuse
senses.meaning: Justifies your own behavior in a pouty or defiant way. Often paired with 「だって」. Mostly used by women and children in speech; 「もん」 is more casual.
senses.connection: だって + plain form／〜んだ + もん (もの)
examples: But I didn't know!
But I'm still sleepy!

senses.label: Reason seeking agreement
senses.meaning: Gives a reason and hopes the listener will understand or agree: “after all, it's ...”. Often 「〜だもの、〜」 or 「〜だもんね」.
senses.connection: Noun／な-adj. + だもの・だもん (ね)
examples: They're just a kid. It can't be helped.
It's your first time, after all. Of course it didn't go perfectly.

notes: It is childish and coquettish, used only among intimates such as family and friends. Saying 「知らなかったんだもん」 to a superior or client is very rude; say 「存じ上げませんでした。申し訳ありません」.
Adults using it at work sound childish and irresponsible. To give a reason, use 「〜ので」 or 「〜ものですから」.
Connection: nouns and な-adjectives take 「だ」 (○「子供だもの」, 「初めてだもん」), verbs and い-adjectives mostly take 「んだ」 (○「眠いんだもん」); ✕「子供もん」.

daily.title: A child's excuse
daily.description: A child hasn't done their homework and makes excuses to mom.
daily.example: But the homework is too hard!

daily.title: Being sweet with a partner
daily.description: A girlfriend explains why she got jealous.
daily.example: But I was lonely!

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend's first try at cooking went wrong, and you reassure them.
daily.example: It's your first time. It's fine if it doesn't work out.

work.title: Casual chat with coworkers
work.description: A light remark between close coworkers. Not for formal settings.
work.example: It's Friday, after all. Of course you want to go home early.

etymology: It comes from 「もの」 at the end of sentences like 「ものだ」 and 「ものを」 being used on its own. 「もの」 presents the reason as an established fact, giving an excuse-like tone of “it can't be helped”. 「もん」 is the spoken form.

similar.title: 〜ものだから
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜ものだから」 joins cause and result mid-sentence and can be used for a fairly polite excuse; sentence-final 「〜もん」 is more colloquial and coquettish.

similar.title: 〜もので
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜もので」 comes mid-sentence and is quite polite, so it works in business apologies; sentence-final 「〜もん」 is for intimates only.

similar.title: 〜のだから・〜んだから
similar.explanation: Sentence-final 「〜んだから」 also stresses the reason (「だって忙しかったんだから」), more strongly and with some resentment, but not coquettishly. When adults explain a reason, it is more natural than 「〜もん」.

formation: The usual account is that this 「もの」 was the formal noun in sentence endings such as 「〜ものを」 or 「〜ものだ」, and what followed dropped off, leaving it alone at the end of the sentence. 「もの」 presents the preceding reason as “an established fact, simply how things are”, implying “I can't help it”. So 「知らなかったんだもの」 has the excusing tone of “I just didn't know, so don't blame me”. 「んだ」 often comes before it to stress “that's how it is”, and it often pairs with 「だって」 to make a sulky, coquettish tone. 「もん」 is the spoken contraction and sounds even more childish.

meaning: Lists a few examples out of many things or situations, implying there are more. Often suggests “so much going on, it's a mess”.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form／い-adj. + やら + noun／verb dictionary form／い-adj. + やら

senses.label: Listing things
senses.meaning: Lists several things: “... and ... and so on”. Often suggests clutter, too many things, or being busy.
senses.connection: Noun + やら + noun + やら (で／が／を)
examples: My desk is piled high with books, documents and whatnot.
I'm busy getting ready to move, with cleaning, packing and everything.

senses.label: Mixed emotions
senses.meaning: Lists several feelings or states that happen at once, showing complex feelings that are hard to put into words: “both ... and ...”.
senses.connection: い-adj.／verb dictionary form + やら + い-adj.／verb dictionary form + やら
examples: Hearing my son is getting married, I feel happy and lonely at the same time. It's complicated.
Being praised in front of everyone all of a sudden, I was so surprised and embarrassed that my face turned red.

notes: It gives an impression of “so many and so messy that one can't cope”, so it does not suit a neutral list in a formal report: ✕「資料には売上やら利益やらを載せました」 → ○「資料には売上や利益などを載せました」.
With emotions, it usually describes contrasting or tangled feelings (「嬉しいやら寂しいやら」); listing only a single positive emotion sounds unnatural.
The 「やら」 in 「どうやら」, 「何やら」, 「誰やら」 expresses uncertainty and is not a list: 「どうやら雨らしい」 means “it seems it's going to rain”.
Verbs and い-adjectives take 「やら」 directly in the dictionary form (○「驚くやら照れるやら」); do not change it to the て-form.

daily.title: Complaining about being busy
daily.description: Too much to do at the end of the year, and you vent to a friend.
daily.example: With the big year-end cleaning, New Year's cards and everything, I don't even have time to rest.

daily.title: Telling about a bad day
daily.description: Telling your family about your bad luck when you get home.
daily.example: I got caught in the rain, lost my wallet... Today was awful.

daily.title: Reading an essay
daily.description: An essay writer describes mixed feelings.
daily.example: Back in my hometown after a long time, I felt nostalgic and lonely all at once, and my heart was full.

work.title: Explaining a hectic day
work.description: The day before an event, telling a coworker how much prep is left.
work.example: Between setting up the venue and printing the handouts, it looks like I'll be working late today.

etymology: Generally thought to come from the old phrase 「にやあらむ」 (“perhaps it is ...”), which changed through 「やらん」 into 「やら」. It first expressed uncertainty, then came to be used for lists, hinting at “other things too”.

similar.title: 〜とか〜とか
similar.explanation: 「〜とか〜とか」 is a neutral spoken list that fits any situation. 「〜やら〜やら」 often carries a sense of “a great many, hectic, mixed feelings”.

similar.title: 〜だの〜だの
similar.explanation: 「〜だの〜だの」 also lists, but is mostly used to report someone's complaints or excuses, with the speaker's annoyance or criticism (「高いだの遠いだの文句ばかり」). 「〜やら〜やら」 focuses on a tangle of things or mixed feelings.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 「〜たり〜たり」 only lists representative actions with the た-form of verbs and has no particular emotion. 「〜やら〜やら」 can follow nouns and adjectives and stresses disorder or tangled feelings.

similar.title: 〜のやら〜のやら
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「やら」 originally means “uncertain”. 「〜のやら〜のやら」 means “whether ... or ...” (「本気なのやら冗談なのやら」), expressing puzzlement, while 「〜やら〜やら」 is a list.

formation: 「やら」 is generally thought to be a contraction of 「にやあらん」 (“I wonder if it's ...”), and its original meaning is “uncertainty”. Lining up such vague things, “... and ..., and the like”, implies “and other things I can't list in full”. Precisely because they can't be fully listed or sorted out, it naturally gives the feeling of “many, messy, overwhelming”. Used with emotions, it means several feelings flooding in at once, so mixed that you can't say which is which: “both ... and ...”.

meaning: Imagines an undesirable situation: “if things are like this, (it's no good)”. The second half is a negative judgment or result.
connection: Verb dictionary form／nai-form／ている form, noun + の + ようでは (casual: ようじゃ)

senses.label: Criticism
senses.meaning: Points out someone's poor behavior and criticizes it: “if you're like this, it won't do”. The second half is often a negative evaluation like 「〜とは言えない」, 「無理だ」 or 「失格だ」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／nai-form／ている form + ようでは、〜 (negative evaluation)
examples: If you make such a simple mistake, you can't call yourself a pro.
If you can't get up in the morning, you're not fit to be a working adult.
If this tires you out, there's no way you can climb a mountain.

senses.label: Worry / warning
senses.meaning: Supposes that a bad situation continues or happens and predicts a bad result: “if ..., then probably ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／nai-form + ようでは、〜だろう／〜必要がある
examples: If the rain keeps up like this, the game will probably be canceled.
If sales don't grow, we'll need to rethink the plan.

notes: The second clause must be a negative judgment or result, never a positive one: ✕「毎日練習するようでは、きっと上手になる」 → ○「毎日練習すれば、きっと上手になる」.
It is often used to criticize the listener directly (「こんなミスをするようでは困る」) and is quite harsh. To a superior or colleague it sounds like scolding, so use a gentler reminder.
「〜(よ)うではないか」 after the volitional form is a call to action, “let's ...” (「みんなで頑張ろうではないか」), unrelated to this grammar point; watch the verb form before it.

daily.title: A parent scolds a child
daily.description: A child is still playing games right before an exam.
daily.example: If all you do is play games before the exam, you won't pass.

daily.title: Advice between friends
daily.description: A friend is always late, and another friend warns them.
daily.example: If you're late every time, people will stop trusting you.

work.title: A boss criticizes
work.description: A report is full of mistakes, and the boss points it out sharply.
work.example: It's a problem if you can't even spot the mistakes in your own report.

work.title: Analysis in a meeting
work.description: Discussing how to deal with poor results in a management meeting.
work.example: If we ignore what customers say, we can't win against the competition.

etymology: 「よう」 (様, appearance) plus the conditional 「では」. Literally “if it's in that state”. Because it was used so much for criticism and warnings, it became fixed as a pattern leading to a negative result.

similar.title: 〜ては・〜ていては（仮定・マイナスの結果）
similar.explanation: 「〜ては」 takes an action directly as the condition for a bad result (「そんなに食べては太るよ」). 「〜ようでは」 adds 「よう」 and judges the other's behavior as a “state”, so the criticism and disappointment are stronger.

similar.title: 〜ていては
similar.explanation: 「〜ていては」 stresses that continuing in this way will lead to a bad result (「遊んでいては合格できない」). 「〜ようでは」 focuses on a negative evaluation of the current performance.

similar.title: 〜ようなら
similar.explanation: Same origin, also 「よう」 + conditional. 「〜ようなら」 is a neutral condition, and the second clause can be advice or instruction (「熱が下がらないようなら、病院へ行きなさい」); 「〜ようでは」 allows only a negative evaluation.

formation: 「ようでは」 is 「よう（様）」, meaning appearance or manner, plus 「で」, the continuative form of 「だ」, plus the topic particle 「は」. 「よう」 turns the preceding action into “a state of ...”, and 「では」 means “if it is ...”, so together “if it is in such a state ...”. Treating the other person's behavior as a “state” to suppose already carries an assessing, evaluating eye, and 「は」 adds contrast and limitation, hinting “that won't do”, so the second clause is always a negative conclusion. In speech 「では」 contracts to 「じゃ」, giving 「ようじゃ」.

meaning: Says a certain difference doesn't matter: “regardless of ...”, “whether ... or ...”. Mostly used in writing, job ads and notices.
connection: Noun + を問わず (「は問わない」, 「は問いません」)

senses.label: Regardless of
senses.meaning: The difference in the first part doesn't matter; the second part applies either way. Usually follows words that contain opposites or a range, such as 「男女」, 「昼夜」, 「年齢」, 「国籍」 or 「有無」.
senses.connection: Noun (「男女」, 「昼夜」, 「年齢」, 「国内外」, etc.) + を問わず
examples: Anyone can apply for this job, regardless of age or experience.
Many people took part in this event, regardless of nationality.
Construction continues day and night.

senses.label: Not required
senses.meaning: 「〜は問いません」 says something is not a condition or requirement. A set phrase in job ads and notices.
senses.connection: Noun + は問いません／は問わない
examples: No education requirements.
Experience not required.

notes: It must follow a noun that contains “differences or a range” (「男女」, 「年齢」, 「昼夜」, 「経験の有無」); a single concrete noun does not work: ✕「田中さんを問わず」.
It cannot follow a verb directly: ✕「参加するを問わず」 → ○「参加するかどうかを問わず」 or 「参加する・しないにかかわらず」.
In job ads, 「学歴不問」 and 「学歴は問いません」 mean “educational background doesn't matter”, not “you may not ask about it”; do not misread them.
It is written language. In everyday conversation 「年齢を問わず」 sounds stiff; speakers more often say 「年齢に関係なく」.

daily.title: Reading a job ad
daily.description: You see a part-time job poster at a convenience store.
daily.example: Part-timers wanted! Any age, no experience needed.

daily.title: Recommending a spot
daily.description: Telling a friend about a place that's fun all year round.
daily.example: That park is fun no matter what season you go.

work.title: A company job posting
work.description: HR announces a job opening.
work.example: Regardless of nationality, we welcome motivated applicants.

work.title: A news report
work.description: The news talks about how popular a product is.
work.example: This product is popular with men and women across a wide range of ages.

etymology: The verb 「問う」 (to ask, to question) in the form 「問わ」 plus the classical negative 「ず」. Literally “without asking”. It came to mean “not treating ... as an issue or condition”.

similar.title: 〜にかかわらず
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning. 「〜にかかわらず」 can also follow opposed pairs such as 「行く行かない」 or 「晴雨」 and verbs; 「〜を問わず」 generally follows only nouns and is more common in job ads and notices.

similar.title: 〜によらず
similar.explanation: 「〜によらず」 also means “regardless of ...” (「性別によらず採用する」), but can also mean “not relying on (a means)”; 「〜を問わず」 only means “not treating ... as a condition”.

similar.title: 〜いかんにかかわらず／〜いかんを問わず
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜いかんを問わず」 is a stiffer N1 expression meaning “regardless of the content or circumstances of ...” (「理由のいかんを問わず」), mostly used in regulations and contracts.

formation: 「を問わず」 is the irrealis stem 「問わ」 of the verb 「問う」 (to ask, to inquire into) plus the classical negative 「ず」; literally “without inquiring into ...”. In recruitment or regulations, “inquiring into” a point means examining it as a qualification or condition, so “not inquiring” means “not treating it as a condition”, that is, “regardless of ..., anyone is fine”. Since what is “inquired into” is a distinction or criterion, the noun before it is one that itself contains many possibilities, such as 「男女」, 「年齢」 or 「有無」. 「ず」 is classical negation, so the phrase has an official, written tone; in speech people say 「は問いません」 or 「に関係なく」 instead.

meaning: Something becomes the starting point or trigger for a later change or action: “... led to ...”, “ever since ...”.
connection: Noun／verb plain form + の + をきっかけに (して)／がきっかけで

senses.label: Triggered by
senses.meaning: Some chance event becomes the starting point of a new action or change: “thanks to ...”, “ever since ...”. Works in both speech and writing.
senses.connection: Noun + をきっかけに／をきっかけにして／をきっかけとして
examples: Studying abroad got me interested in Japanese culture.
Coming across a certain book made me want to become a writer.

senses.label: ... was the trigger
senses.meaning: Makes the trigger the subject: “... was what started ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + がきっかけで／がきっかけとなって
examples: A comment from a friend got me to start dieting.
That incident led to a change in the law.

notes: The clause after it must be a new action or change that starts from this point (「〜ようになった」, 「〜始めた」), not a one-time direct result: ✕「地震をきっかけに、家が倒れた」 → ○「地震で家が倒れた」.
「きっかけ」 means “a start”, not “a cause”. To simply give a cause use 「〜で」 or 「〜ため」; with 「きっかけ」 it becomes “from this, ... began”.
Be careful about presenting someone else's misfortune as a trigger. Telling disaster victims 「震災をきっかけに町が良くなった」 can seem insensitive to what they went through.

daily.title: How a hobby started
daily.description: A friend asks why you started playing guitar.
daily.example: I started playing guitar because of the school festival in high school.

daily.title: Love stories
daily.description: A friend asks how a couple met.
daily.example: We started dating after taking the same class.

daily.title: Changing habits
daily.description: Telling a friend why you started running.
daily.example: After my health checkup results, I started running every morning.

work.title: A job interview
work.description: A candidate explains their motivation to the interviewer.
work.example: My internship got me interested in the work your company does.

work.title: A news report
work.description: Reporting social change caused by an event.
work.example: This accident led to a review of safety standards.

etymology: 「きっかけ」 is generally thought to come from 「切り掛け」, the stem of the verb 「切り掛ける」, with a sound change. It originally meant “the beginning, a place to start”, and later “the cause or chance that starts something”.

similar.title: 〜を契機に
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning. 「〜を契機に」 is a Sino-Japanese word, more formal, mostly for big social or historical turning points; 「〜をきっかけに」 is common in speech too and fits small personal matters.

similar.title: 〜を機に
similar.explanation: 「〜を機に」 stresses “taking advantage of the occasion” to actively do something, and what precedes is mostly a life milestone such as marriage, retirement or moving (「退職を機に田舎へ移る」). 「〜をきっかけに」 mostly refers to a change that arises naturally from the trigger.

similar.title: 〜を皮切りに
similar.explanation: Both relate to “starting points”. 「〜を皮切りに」 means “starting with ..., similar things follow one after another” (「東京を皮切りに全国で公演する」); the next clause is not a change but a series of similar events.

formation: 「をきっかけに」 is the noun 「きっかけ」 plus the case particle 「を」 plus 「に（して）」. 「AをBにする」 means “make A into B”, so 「〜をきっかけにする」 is “take ... as the start”. 「きっかけ」 is generally thought to come from 「切り掛け」, “the place where you begin cutting, the beginning of a matter”. Since it is a “beginning”, what follows is naturally a new action or change that starts from there, not a one-time result. When the trigger itself is the subject, use 「〜がきっかけで」 or 「〜がきっかけとなって」, “... became the start”.

meaning: Written style. Something becomes a turning point that brings major change or new development: “taking ... as an opportunity”.
connection: Noun + を契機に (して)／を契機として／が契機となって

senses.label: Turning point
senses.meaning: An event becomes a turning point that brings major change to society, an organization or a person. More formal than 「きっかけ」, used in news, papers and speeches.
senses.connection: Noun + を契機に／を契機として／を契機にして
examples: The great earthquake raised awareness of disaster prevention.
The Tokyo Olympics pushed forward barrier-free design in the city.

senses.label: ... became the turning point
senses.meaning: Makes the turning point the subject: “... became the trigger for ...”. Common in news and reports.
senses.connection: Noun + が契機となり／が契機となって
examples: This discovery led to the development of a new treatment.

notes: It is written language. In daily conversation 「留学を契機に…」 sounds stiff; in speech use 「〜をきっかけに」.
The second clause is a major change or new development; do not use it for trivial things: ✕「雨を契機に傘を買った」 → ○「雨が降ったので傘を買った」.
「契機（けいき）」 sounds the same as 「景気」 (the economic climate); do not confuse them in writing: 「景気回復を契機に」 means “with the economic recovery as the turning point”.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report explains the background of a new policy.
daily.example: Prompted by the falling birthrate, child-rearing support measures were expanded.

daily.title: Reading a biography
daily.description: A biography describes a turning point in someone's life.
daily.example: His father's death led him to decide to take over the family business.

work.title: A CEO's speech
work.description: A speech at the company's anniversary celebration.
work.example: With our 50th anniversary as a turning point, we will take on new businesses.

work.title: An academic paper
work.description: A paper discusses historical change.
work.example: With the Meiji Restoration, Japan's modernization began in earnest.

etymology: 「契機」 is a Sino-Japanese word: 「契」 suggests “fitting together”, and 「機」 means “moment, key point”. One theory says it spread after the Meiji era as a translation of the philosophical term “Moment” (German), and later came to mean “a key factor that brings change”.

similar.title: 〜をきっかけに
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning. 「〜をきっかけに」 works in both speech and writing, and the trigger can be a small personal matter; 「〜を契機に」 is more formal and mostly refers to social or larger changes.

similar.title: 〜を機に
similar.explanation: 「〜を機に」 stresses actively doing something “taking advantage of the occasion”, often after 「退職」 or 「結婚」; 「〜を契機に」 focuses on “change brought about by this”. Both contain 「機」 and are often interchangeable in writing.

similar.title: 〜を皮切りに
similar.explanation: Both relate to “starting points”. 「〜を皮切りに」 means similar activities unfold one after another from a start (「東京を皮切りに全国で公演」), and it does not express a change.

formation: 「を契機に」 is the Sino-Japanese noun 「契機」 plus 「を」 plus 「に（して）／として」. 「AをBにする／Bとする」 means “make A into B”, so 「〜を契機に」 is “take ... as the turning point”. One account says 「契機」 was a Meiji-period rendering of the German word Moment, originally “a decisive factor that drives change”, so it is more abstract and more formal than the native word 「きっかけ」. Since the “turning point” is a factor that drives change, the second clause is always a resulting change or new development, often a big one at the social or organizational level.

meaning: Shows that something is done through a person or thing as a medium or means. Can also mean “throughout” a whole period or area.
connection: Noun + を通じて／を通して (before a noun: を通じた／を通した)

senses.label: Through (a medium)
senses.meaning: Something is achieved through a person, a method or an experience: “through ...”. 「を通じて」 is more formal; 「を通して」 is also common in speech.
senses.connection: Noun (person・media・activity, etc.) + を通じて／を通して／を通じた + noun
examples: I met her through a friend.
Through the internet, you can get information from all over the world.
Interaction through social media is spreading.

senses.label: Throughout
senses.meaning: After a noun of time or area: “throughout the whole ...”, “all ... long”.
senses.connection: Time・area noun (「一年」, 「生涯」, 「全国」, etc.) + を通じて／を通して
examples: This region is mild all year round.
He called for peace throughout his life.

notes: In the passive, the agent takes 「によって」; with 「を通じて」 the meaning becomes “conveyed through someone”: ✕「この小説は村上春樹を通じて書かれた」 → ○「村上春樹によって書かれた」.
The time sense follows only words for a span (「一年」, 「生涯」, 「四季」) and means “throughout the whole period”; it does not follow a point in time: ✕「三時を通じて」.
The 「通す」 in 「目を通す」 (look over), 「火を通す」 (cook through) and 「話を通す」 (put in a word beforehand) is a full verb, not this grammar point.
In Japanese business, contacting a company formally often goes through an introducer (「〇〇さんを通じてご連絡します」); skipping the introducer to contact them directly can sometimes be seen as rude.

daily.title: How you met
daily.description: Telling a friend how you met your boyfriend.
daily.example: We met through a mutual friend.

daily.title: Recommending a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend about Okinawa's weather.
daily.example: Okinawa is warm all year round, so you can go anytime.

work.title: Contact through an agent
work.description: Telling a client you'll contact them through an agency.
work.example: We will contact you with details through our agency.

work.title: Annual report
work.description: Summing up the year's results in a report.
work.example: Over the fiscal year as a whole, sales exceeded last year's.

work.title: Training wrap-up
work.description: A new employee shares what they learned from training.
work.example: Through this training, I learned the importance of teamwork.

etymology: 「通じる」 (classical 「通ず」) and 「通す」 both mean “to pass through”. From “passing through something to the other side” came “via a medium”, and from “running from start to end” came “throughout a period”.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: 「〜によって」 focuses on the means or method itself, or the agent (「機械によって作る」). 「〜を通じて」 focuses on going “through an intermediary”, and what precedes is often a person or a channel of communication.

similar.title: 〜にわたって
similar.explanation: Both can express a time range. 「〜にわたって」 stresses the breadth of the range or length of time (「十年にわたって調査する」); 「〜を通じて」 stresses that a state continues “all the way through” (「一年を通じて温暖だ」).

similar.title: 〜を経て
similar.explanation: 「〜を経て」 means arriving at the next step after passing through a place, stage or procedure (「審査を経て決定する」), stressing the order; 「〜を通じて」 stresses using an intermediary or running from beginning to end.

similar.title: 〜通す
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「通す」, “carry through from start to finish”. 「〜通す」 follows the ます-stem of a verb and means “carry the action through to the end” (「最後まで走り通す」); 「〜を通して」 follows a noun and means an intermediary or a whole period.

formation: It is the case particle 「を」 plus the て-form of the verb 「通じる」 or 「通す」. The core meaning of both verbs is “pass through from one end to the other”. Used with people, media or activities, it means “passing through this intermediary to reach the goal”, hence “through ...”; used with time such as 「一年」 or 「生涯」, it means “running from start to finish”, hence “throughout the period”. 「通じる」 is intransitive (things go through naturally) and 「通す」 is transitive (making it go through), so 「を通して」 carries a slightly “deliberately making use of” nuance, while 「を通じて」 is more neutral and written.

meaning: Leaves something out: “except for ...”. More formal and written than 「以外」.
connection: Noun + を除いて／を除き／を除けば (before a noun: を除く)

senses.label: Except
senses.meaning: Leaves out one part; the rest is covered by the second half: “everything except ...”. Notices and written texts often use 「を除き」 or 「を除く」.
senses.connection: Noun + を除いて／を除き、〜; noun + を除く + noun
examples: We're open every day except Sunday.
It will be sunny across the country, except in some areas.
Everyone except Tanaka agreed.

senses.label: Only ... (with a negative)
senses.meaning: 「〜を除いては〜ない」 and 「〜を除けば」 stress “no one/nothing other than this” or “apart from this point, it's fine”.
senses.connection: Noun + を除いては〜ない; noun + を除けば、〜
examples: Nobody but him knows the secret.
Apart from this point, the plan is perfect.

notes: In notices, 「土日・祝日を除く」 means “weekends and holidays not included”, so mind it when counting deadlines: the real number of days for 「5営業日以内（土日祝を除く）」 is longer than 5.
It is fairly formal. In daily conversation 「日曜日を除いて」 sounds stiff; 「〜以外」 is more natural in speech.
Before a noun use 「〜を除く＋noun」 (「日曜日を除く毎日」, 「田中さんを除く全員」), not 「〜を除いての」.
「除く」 also has the literal meaning “remove”: 「種を除いてから切る」 (remove the seeds, then cut) does not mean “except”.

daily.title: Talking about food
daily.description: A friend asks if there's anything you can't eat.
daily.example: Apart from spicy food, I can eat anything.

daily.title: Reading a shop sign
daily.description: A sign on a shop door shows the opening days.
daily.example: Open every day of the year except over the New Year holidays.

work.title: Sending a notice
work.description: The general affairs department announces who takes part in an event.
work.example: This applies to all employees except managers.

work.title: Weather forecast
work.description: A forecast describes the weather around the country.
work.example: Rain is expected across the country, except in Hokkaido.

etymology: From the verb 「除く」 (to remove, to exclude), originally “to take something away”. 「を除いて」 means “after taking ... away (the rest)”, that is, “except for ...”.

similar.title: 〜をおいて
similar.explanation: 「〜をおいて」 is followed by a negative and means “there is no one more suitable than ...”, used for high praise (「彼をおいて適任者はいない」). 「〜を除いて」 neutrally leaves something out.

similar.title: 〜抜きで・〜抜きにして
similar.explanation: 「〜抜きで」 means “without ...” (「わさび抜きで」, 「冗談抜きで」), focusing on doing something with a component removed; 「〜を除いて」 focuses on “apart from this part, all the rest ...”.

similar.title: 〜は別として
similar.explanation: 「〜は別として」 means “... is another matter”, putting something outside the discussion for now (「費用は別として、計画はいい」); 「〜を除いて」 explicitly excludes it from the scope of what follows.

formation: It is the case particle 「を」 plus the て-form of the verb 「除く」 (to remove, to exclude); literally “after removing ...”. “After removing a part, all the rest ...” becomes “everything except ...”. With 「を除いては〜ない」 it is “once that is removed, there is none”, stressing uniqueness; with 「を除けば」 it is “if you take that point away”, leading into an evaluation of the rest. The 中止形 「を除き」 and the attributive form 「を除く」 are written forms, common in notices and manuals.

meaning: Uses something as the material, basis or source for creating or judging: “based on ...”.
connection: Noun + をもとに (して)／をもとにした + noun／がもとになって

senses.label: Based on
senses.meaning: Uses something as material, reference or basis to create, make or judge something. Often used with verbs like 「作る」, 「書く」 or 「開発する」. Written in kanji as 「元」 or 「基」.
senses.connection: Noun + をもとに／をもとにして／をもとにした + noun
examples: This movie is based on a true story.
We developed a new product based on the survey results.
A novel based on real events is getting a lot of attention.

senses.label: ... became the basis
senses.meaning: Makes the source the subject: “... became the basis or model for ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + がもとになって／がもとになった
examples: This story was born from my grandfather's wartime experiences.

notes: 「〜をもとに」 lets you freely work on the material, while 「〜に基づいて」 requires following it strictly without deviation. Telling a superior 「規則をもとに処理しました」 is understood as “I handled it at my discretion, using the rules as reference”; say 「規則に基づいて処理しました」.
The kanji can be 「元」 or 「基」: 「基」 is common for a basis such as data or facts, and 「元」 for material or a prototype. The 「元」 in 「元に戻す」 (restore) means “original”, not this grammar point.
Before a noun use 「〜をもとにした＋noun」: ○「実話をもとにした映画」; ✕「実話をもとにの映画」.

daily.title: Talking about a drama
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about an adaptation.
daily.example: I heard this drama is based on a popular manga.

daily.title: Home cooking
daily.description: Explaining how you cook a dish.
daily.example: I used my mom's recipe as a base and gave it my own twist.

work.title: Explaining a proposal
work.description: Explaining the basis of a new plan in a meeting.
work.example: We built our sales strategy based on customer data.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: Stating the data source in a report.
work.example: This report was prepared based on last year's survey results.

etymology: 「もと」 can be written 「元」, 「基」 or 「本」, and originally means “root, foundation, origin”. 「〜をもとに」 literally means “taking ... as the foundation”, hence “based on ...”.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: Both mean “based on”. 「〜に基づいて」 stresses following rules, facts or data strictly without deviating (「法律に基づいて判断する」); 「〜をもとに」 takes the material as a starting point and allows free processing and creation.

similar.title: 〜を踏まえて
similar.explanation: 「〜を踏まえて」 means “taking ... fully into account, and going further” (「前回の反省を踏まえて計画を立てる」), stressing putting the premise into consideration; 「〜をもとに」 stresses treating something as raw material or a starting point.

similar.title: 〜に沿って
similar.explanation: 「〜に沿って」 means “following (a policy or expectation) and staying consistent with it” (「会社の方針に沿って進める」); 「〜をもとに」 only says it is the basis, and what follows can be developed freely.

formation: It is the noun 「もと（元・基）」 plus 「を」 plus 「に（する）」. 「AをBにする」 means “make A into B”, and 「もと」 is “foundation, source”, so 「〜をもとにする」 is “take ... as the foundation or starting point”. Since it is only a “starting point”, you can process, create and develop on top of it, so the second clause is often 「作る」, 「書く」 or 「開発する」; this is why it is freer than 「〜に基づいて」 (stand on it without leaving it). When the material is the subject, use 「〜がもとになって」, “... became the foundation or prototype”.
